prompt: For an ideal gas on a reversible adiabatic path, the section writes dŪ = δq + δw = 0 − P dV̄. Why is dŪ negative during an expansion?

choices.text: dV̄ is positive, so −P dV̄ is negative
δq is negative, because heat leaves the gas
choices.why: δq = 0 on an adiabatic path. The sign comes from the work term: dV̄ > 0 in an expansion, so −P dV̄ < 0.

choices.text: P becomes negative as the gas expands
choices.why: Pressure is always positive. dŪ is negative because dV̄ is positive in an expansion, which makes −P dV̄ negative.

choices.text: dV̄ is negative, because the gas expands
choices.why: In an expansion the volume grows, so dV̄ is positive. With the minus sign in −P dV̄, dŪ then comes out negative.

explanation: With δq = 0, the only term left is the work, δw = −P dV̄. In an expansion dV̄ > 0 and P > 0, so dŪ < 0: the gas loses internal energy.

prompt: In a reversible adiabatic expansion, the molar internal energy Ū of an ideal gas goes down. Why does that mean its temperature goes down?

choices.text: Since dŪ = C̄_V dT, Ū can fall only if T falls
A larger volume lowers Ū even at a fixed T
choices.why: For an ideal gas Ū depends on T alone, through dŪ = C̄_V dT. The only way for Ū to fall is for T to fall.

choices.text: Heat flows out of the gas as Ū goes down
choices.why: No heat flows on an adiabatic path. Ū falls because the gas does work, and since dŪ = C̄_V dT, T falls with it.

choices.text: The pressure rises, and a higher pressure cools a gas
choices.why: The pressure falls in an expansion. T drops because Ū drops and, for an ideal gas, dŪ = C̄_V dT.

explanation: For an ideal gas, Ū changes only with temperature: dŪ = C̄_V dT, with C̄_V > 0. So when the work done by the gas lowers Ū, T must fall too.

prompt: The section turns C̄_V dT = −P dV̄ into C̄_V dT = −(RT/V̄) dV̄. Which relation does it use for this step?

choices.text: The ideal gas law, P = RT/V̄ for one mole
The heat capacity relation R = C̄_P − C̄_V
choices.why: That relation comes later, to write the exponent as γ − 1. Here P is replaced using the ideal gas law, P = RT/V̄.

choices.text: The definition C̄_V = ((∂Ū)/(∂T))_V
choices.why: That definition gives dŪ = C̄_V dT, the left side. To replace P, the section uses the ideal gas law, P = RT/V̄.

choices.text: The condition that T stays constant
choices.why: T does not stay constant along an adiabat; it falls. The step simply replaces P with RT/V̄ from the ideal gas law.

explanation: For one mole of an ideal gas, PV̄ = RT, so P = RT/V̄. Putting this in gives C̄_V dT = −(RT/V̄) dV̄, which holds only for an ideal gas.

prompt: Why does the section divide by T to get ((C̄_V)/T) dT = −(R/V̄) dV̄?

choices.text: To separate the variables T and V̄
To hold T constant during the expansion
choices.why: T is not held constant; it falls. Dividing by T puts all the T terms on the left and all the V̄ terms on the right.

choices.text: To remove C̄_V from the equation
choices.why: C̄_V is still there on the left. The division separates the variables so that each side can be integrated on its own.

choices.text: To turn the expansion into a compression
choices.why: Dividing by T doesn't change the process. It separates the variables, with T on the left and V̄ on the right.

explanation: Before dividing, the right side −(RT/V̄) dV̄ still contains T. Dividing by T leaves only T on the left and only V̄ on the right, so each side can be integrated over its own variable.

prompt: The section writes its result as T_2/T_1 = (V_1/V_2)^(γ − 1). What is γ?

choices.text: C̄_P/C̄_V, the ratio of the two heat capacities
C̄_V/C̄_P, the ratio of the two heat capacities
choices.why: That is the ratio upside down. γ = C̄_P/C̄_V, which is larger than 1, so γ − 1 is positive.

choices.text: C̄_P − C̄_V, the difference of the heat capacities
choices.why: For an ideal gas that difference is R. γ is the ratio C̄_P/C̄_V, and γ − 1 = R/C̄_V.

choices.text: R/C̄_V, the gas constant over the heat capacity
choices.why: R/C̄_V is γ − 1, not γ itself. γ = C̄_P/C̄_V.

explanation: γ = C̄_P/C̄_V, the ratio of the molar heat capacities at constant pressure and at constant volume. Since C̄_P is larger than C̄_V, γ > 1 and the exponent γ − 1 is positive.

prompt: Why can the exponent R/C̄_V be rewritten as γ − 1, with γ = C̄_P/C̄_V?

choices.text: For an ideal gas, R = C̄_P − C̄_V
For an ideal gas, R = C̄_V
choices.why: C̄_V is not equal to R; for a monatomic gas it is (3/2)R. The step uses R = C̄_P − C̄_V instead.

choices.text: For an ideal gas, C̄_P = C̄_V
choices.why: If the two were equal, γ − 1 would be zero and the gas would not cool. For an ideal gas they differ by R.

choices.text: For an ideal gas, R = C̄_P + C̄_V
choices.why: The heat capacities differ by R; they do not add up to it. With R = C̄_P − C̄_V, R/C̄_V = γ − 1.

explanation: Using R = C̄_P − C̄_V, R/C̄_V = (C̄_P − C̄_V)/(C̄_V) = C̄_P/C̄_V − 1 = γ − 1.

prompt: The section's result T_2/T_1 = (V_1/V_2)^(γ − 1), with γ − 1 > 0, links T and V along a reversible adiabat. What does it show?

choices.text: As the volume increases, the temperature decreases
As the volume increases, the temperature increases
choices.why: When V_2 > V_1, the ratio V_1/V_2 is less than 1, and so is any positive power of it. So T_2 < T_1: the temperature falls.

choices.text: The temperature doesn't depend on the volume
choices.why: T_2/T_1 changes with V_1/V_2, so T does depend on V along the adiabat. A larger volume gives a lower temperature.

choices.text: The temperature is proportional to the volume
choices.why: The formula has V_1/V_2, upside down from V_2/V_1, raised to the power γ − 1. T falls as V grows.

explanation: For an expansion V_1/V_2 < 1, and raising it to the positive power γ − 1 still gives a number below 1. So T_2 < T_1: volume and temperature are inversely related along the adiabat.

prompt: Two ideal gases expand reversibly and adiabatically from the same T_1 by the same volume ratio. Gas X has a larger C̄_V than gas Y. Using T_2/T_1 = (V_1/V_2)^(1/c), with c = C̄_V/R, which gas ends up colder?

choices.text: Gas Y, whose smaller C̄_V gives a larger exponent
Gas X, whose larger C̄_V gives a larger exponent
choices.why: The exponent is 1/c = R/C̄_V, so a larger C̄_V gives a smaller exponent and less cooling. Gas Y, with the smaller C̄_V, cools more.

choices.text: Both end at the same temperature T_2
choices.why: T_2 depends on the exponent R/C̄_V, which differs between the gases. The gas with the smaller C̄_V, gas Y, cools more.

choices.text: Neither cools, since no heat leaves either gas
choices.why: No heat leaves, but each gas does work out of its own internal energy, so both cool. Gas Y cools more, because its exponent R/C̄_V is larger.

explanation: The exponent is 1/c = R/C̄_V. For V_1/V_2 < 1, a larger exponent gives a smaller T_2/T_1, so the gas with the smaller C̄_V, gas Y, ends up colder.

prompt: For which process does the section's result T_2/T_1 = (V_1/V_2)^(γ − 1) hold?

choices.text: A reversible adiabatic change of an ideal gas
An isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
choices.why: In an isothermal expansion T_2 = T_1 by definition. The formula is for a reversible adiabatic path, where q = 0 and T changes.

choices.text: An expansion against a fixed external pressure
choices.why: The derivation uses δw = −P dV̄ with the gas's own pressure, which holds on a reversible path. It applies to a reversible adiabatic change of an ideal gas.

choices.text: Heating of an ideal gas at constant volume
choices.why: At constant volume V_1 = V_2, and the formula would give T_2 = T_1, yet heating changes T. The formula is for a reversible adiabatic path.

explanation: The derivation uses δq = 0 (adiabatic), the gas's own pressure in δw = −P dV̄ (reversible), and P = RT/V̄ (ideal gas). It describes a reversible adiabatic expansion or compression of an ideal gas.

prompt: For a monatomic ideal gas such as argon, C̄_V = (3/2)R. What is the exponent R/C̄_V = γ − 1 in T_2/T_1 = (V_1/V_2)^(γ − 1)? (Give it as a decimal.)
A monatomic ideal gas at 360 K expands reversibly and adiabatically to 8 times its starting volume. Using T_2 = T_1 × (V_1/V_2)^(2/3), and the fact that 8^(2/3) = 4, what is T_2, in K?
explanation: V_1/V_2 = 1/8, and (1/8)^(2/3) = 1/4. So T_2 = 360 K × 1/4 = 90 K: the gas cools a lot in this large expansion.

prompt: N2 behaves as an ideal gas with γ − 1 = 0.40. It is compressed reversibly and adiabatically from 300 K to half its starting volume. Using T_2 = T_1 × (V_1/V_2)^(0.40) and 2^(0.40) = 1.32, what is T_2, in K?
explanation: V_1/V_2 = 2, so T_2 = 300 K × 1.32 = 396 K. Compression heats the gas, the reverse of the cooling in an expansion.

prompt: In a small step of a reversible adiabatic expansion, one mole of a monatomic ideal gas does 0.25 J of work, so P dV̄ = 0.25 J/mol. Using C̄_V dT = −P dV̄ with C̄_V = 12.5 J/(mol·K), what is the temperature change dT, in K? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: dT = −P dV̄/C̄_V = −0.25/12.5 K = −0.020 K. The temperature falls, because the work comes out of the internal energy.
